title: Trump Lost in Court After the Pentagon Tried to Choke Reporter Access
description_short: Trump Lost in Court After the Pentagon Tried to Choke Reporter Access
description_medium: A federal judge sided with The New York Times and blocked key parts of the Pentagon policy limiting reporters' access, ruling that the Trump administration's new restrictions were unlawful. This is exactly how press intimidation works in practice: not always one dramatic ban, but a thicket of access rules designed to punish scrutiny and domesticate coverage. When a court has to tell the Pentagon not to play games with the press, the game was already obvious.
description_long: A federal judge sided with The New York Times in its challenge to Pentagon rules limiting reporters' access, blocking key parts of the policy as unlawful, according to PBS NewsHour. The restrictions were adopted by the Trump administration and affected the press corps' ability to report from the Defense Department. The ruling addressed the challenged access policy; it did not end the broader dispute over press access. A separately linked Associated Press report is titled as a later finding that the Pentagon violated an order to restore reporters' access, indicating continued litigation over compliance. The rulings constrained the Pentagon's ability to impose the challenged restrictions and required restoration of reporter access. They resolved the immediate access dispute at that stage, while leaving broader press-pentagon relations outside the court's finding.

title: Signal Chat Leak: Hegseth Shares Yemen Strike Details in Group Including Journalist Jeffrey Goldberg
description_short: Signal Chat Leak: Hegseth Shares Yemen Strike Details in Group Including Journalist Jeffrey Goldberg
description_medium: In March 2025, The Atlantic editor Jeffrey Goldberg was inadvertently included in a Signal chat where senior Trump administration officials discussed a planned U.S. strike in Yemen. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth shared operational details, including targets, timing, and weapons systems, hours before the strike. Officials disputed whether the material was classified.
description_long: In March 2025, The Atlantic editor-in-chief Jeffrey Goldberg reported that he had been inadvertently added to a Signal group chat used by senior Trump administration officials. Participants, including Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, discussed a planned U.S. strike in Yemen, sharing operational details about targets, timing, and weapons systems hours before the operation. Goldberg said he had not requested access and had not identified himself to the group. The incident raised questions about the handling of sensitive military information in a messaging app and about who had access to the conversation. Officials and lawmakers criticized the disclosure as a security risk. Hegseth initially denied the account and later acknowledged the chat, while asserting that no classified information had been shared; the supplied reporting says that characterization was disputed by intelligence and military officials. The record establishes an accidental inclusion and the discussion of operational details, but it does not establish that the leak changed the strike or caused harm to personnel.

title: Assassination of General Qasem Soleimani Without Congressional Authorization
description_short: Assassination of General Qasem Soleimani Without Congressional Authorization
description_medium: On January 3, 2020, President Donald Trump ordered a U.S. drone strike at Baghdad airport that killed Iranian commander Qasem Soleimani and Iraqi militia leader Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis. Congress was not notified in advance. Lawmakers criticized the lack of consultation, and the strike intensified tensions between the United States and Iran.
description_long: On January 3, 2020, a U.S. drone strike at Baghdad International Airport killed Qasem Soleimani, commander of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Quds Force, and Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis, an Iraqi militia leader. President Donald Trump ordered the operation. The administration did not obtain prior congressional authorization or notify congressional leaders before the strike, prompting criticism from lawmakers of both parties and debate about the War Powers Resolution and the president's authority to use force. A classified briefing to lawmakers followed days later; Senator Mike Lee called it the worst briefing he had received on a military issue in nine years. Legal scholars disagreed over whether the killing constituted an act of war. The killing sharply heightened tensions between Washington and Tehran and prompted urgent debate over the risk of further military escalation. The decision also triggered a continuing dispute over the scope of presidential war-making authority and Congress's role.

title: Trump: Federal judge rules against ‘DOGE' in its attempts to seize USIP
description_short: Trump: Federal judge rules against ‘DOGE' in its attempts to seize USIP
description_medium: A federal judge ruled that the Trump administration's removal of the United States Institute of Peace board was unlawful and declared the purported new appointments null and void. The case challenged DOGE and administration officials' effort to take control of the institute. The linked report describes the ruling but not later proceedings.
description_long: In February 2025, Donald Trump issued an executive order declaring the United States Institute of Peace unnecessary and demanding its closure. The institute said it was independent of the executive branch. The next month, Trump fired its board, and DOGE affiliates forcibly removed board members and staff. A U.S. district court judge, Beryl Howell, ruled for the former board and staff, finding the removals unlawful. Howell also declared null and void the administration's claim to USIP's Washington headquarters, described in the linked account as a $500 million property. Court filings say DOGE representatives accompanied by FBI agents had earlier tried to enter the headquarters and were turned away. The defendants included Trump, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the U.S. DOGE Service, and other officials and agencies. The ruling addressed control of the institute and its property; the timeline does not detail subsequent appeals or the final operational status of USIP.

title: Trump: Judge: Trump can't sue NYT for speculating about his ties to Russia
description_short: Trump: Judge: Trump can't sue NYT for speculating about his ties to Russia
description_medium: Manhattan Supreme Court Justice James d'Auguste dismissed with prejudice the Trump campaign's defamation suit against The New York Times over an opinion article about Trump's relationship with Russia. The campaign argued the article suggested allegiance to the Russian government. The dismissal barred refiling that claim; it did not decide the truth of every statement in the article.
description_long: Donald Trump's 2016 campaign sued The New York Times in February 2020 over a 2019 opinion column by former executive editor Max Frankel. The column argued there had been a 'quid pro quo' between the Trump campaign and Russia. The campaign alleged defamation and sought millions of dollars, claiming the article was intended to damage Trump's reelection chances. In March 2021, Manhattan Supreme Court Justice James d'Auguste dismissed the case with prejudice, so the campaign could not refile it. The judge held that Frankel's column was protected opinion, found the complaint did not establish actual malice, and said the campaign lacked standing to sue. The ruling resolved this lawsuit, not the underlying public debate about Russia's role in the 2016 election. A similar campaign suit against CNN had been dismissed, while its case against The Washington Post was pending in federal court. The judge declined the Times' request for monetary sanctions.
